_Story by Katherine Burgess_

Cherie Marceaux lives in Lawrence County, about three hours from Memphis. She
and her husband run an animal rescue with horses, goats, pigs, dogs, ferrets,
and more.

Marceaux says she's not a Democrat or a Republican, but she knows who she
wants to vote for in Tennessee's newly redrawn 9th Congressional District:
Memphis Democrat and State Rep. Justin J. Pearson.

In 2023 Pearson was expelled by Republicans from the state legislature as part
of a protest for tighter gun safety laws with the "Tennessee Three." Instead
of silencing his cause, the expulsion drew national attention and rallied
Memphians around his leadership.

When Tennessee Republicans redrew congressional district lines in May, they
intended to make District 9 a safe Republican seat. In response, Pearson has
focused on issues that appeal to urban and rural voters across the political
spectrum: opposition to data centers, gun safety and the economy. And a recent
poll has him within striking distance of his Republican opponent, State Sen.
Brent Taylor.

"He doesn't just have guts, and he doesn't just call out what's happening, but
he's got hope in his eyes. I can see it in his smile. I can see it in his
face," Marceaux said. "I don't believe in the party system. I believe in
people, and he's a people person. And he's for the environment. How can I not
love him?"

It's unclear whether common ground on these issues will translate to victory
for Pearson in a district that is now heavily Republican and predominantly
white. But regardless of the outcome, Pearson and his supporters say the
coalitions they're creating across District 9 are the first steps to
rebuilding progressive power in Tennessee.

The new District 9 voted for Donald Trump by [more
than](https://www.cookpolitical.com/house/race/485216) 20 points in 2024. The
Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election-rating organization,
[called](https://tennesseelookout.com/2026/09/21/democrats-face-uphill-battle-
in-winning-any-tennessee-u-s-house-race/) the redistricting intended to strip
Tennessee of its last Democratic congressperson "a really effective
gerrymander."

But Pearson supporters think there's a chance. In September, Pearson trailed
Taylor 44% to 48% in a Hart Research poll commissioned by TN Rise PAC and
Three Star PAC (both groups that support Pearson).

"The most powerful thing that's going to come out of this campaign--a win,
lose or draw--[is] that people are realizing their own power," Pearson told
MLK50: Justice Through Journalism in an interview.

"It's been an overwhelming amount of support, overwhelming amount of just love
and power building that I think can change the trajectory of Tennessee
politics," Pearson said. "I think that's what we're going to see not just
after we win, but over the next several years as we continue to build power in
these communities. We're going to be on some county commissions, some school
boards, some mayors. This momentum isn't stopping."

## Data Centers, Environmental Pollution at Core of Pearson Campaign

Marceaux's home county of Lawrence is very different from Memphis. The county
of about 46,000 people is 94% white and largely rural, while Memphis is a
majority Black city of [more than 609,000
residents](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/memphiscitytennessee,US/PST045225).

But both places are grappling with the rapid growth of data centers and
concerns that they'll worsen water, air, and noise pollution. Opposition to
data centers is a unifying position across the 15 counties that form District
9. Voters oppose them by a 36-point margin, according to the Hart Research
poll.

The Pearson campaign has leveraged that opposition to expand his base of
support, stressing that Pearson's record shows he's on the side of the people,
not corporations.

Marceaux said Pearson's longstanding opposition to data centers and other
industrial polluters gives him credibility as he challenges Taylor, who was an
early supporter of Colossus 1 and received [$10,000 in campaign
funding](https://www.fec.gov/data/receipts/?data_type=processed&committee_id=C00949867&contributor_name=C00411116&two_year_transaction_period=2026)
from a political action committee associated with SpaceXAI.

After a 2025 public hearing regarding the data center's gas turbine permits,
Taylor [posted](https://x.com/BrentTaylorTN/status/1916668829880537362) on X,
"I believe our community will unite to embrace this transformative
opportunity."

In 2025, Taylor [passed a
bill](https://wapp.capitol.tn.gov/apps/BillInfo/Default?BillNumber=HB1847&GA=114)
barring municipalities and utility companies from paying for new electrical
infrastructure built to serve a data center. He argued that [the bill would
force](https://www.facebook.com/BrentTaylorTN/posts/tennesseans-shouldnt-
subsidize-big-techs-power-bill-i-wrote-and-passed-the-only-/1068768085770720/)
data centers to pay for their own energy infrastructure, but [critics
say](https://tennesseelookout.com/2026/04/28/tennessee-bill-gives-data-
centers-ability-to-self-power-with-limited-regulation/) the law contains a
loophole that allows the construction of unregulated gas-fired power plants.

Taylor's campaign did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

Just 45 days before the election, Pearson spoke in a small church in the town
of Bolivar, just over an hour outside Memphis. The
[town](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/bolivarcitytennessee/RHI825225)
has just 5,000 residents, about 64% of whom are Black.

"We know we need to stop these toxic data centers from being built in our
communities," he told the room, adding that 67% of future data centers are
planned in rural America "in order to replace our jobs."

Pearson told the room that this fight is personal: He lives three miles from
Colossus 1, the first data center built by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in the Memphis
area.

"People are either worried about the data center that's currently in their
backyard if you're in Whitehaven, or they're worried about what could be
coming to them if you're in Lawrenceburg," Pearson said in an interview.

Bolivar resident Wanda Robinson said she's hopeful that focusing on data
centers will help Pearson overcome the challenges of running in a whiter, more
Republican district.

"If we don't speak out against [data centers], they're liable to do anything,"
Robinson said. "Next thing you know, it may be at our back door. So we have to
stand, speak truth to power."

Pearson has launched two advertisements in the greater Nashville area. Both
mention data centers: "Now I'm running for Congress to stop data centers from
invading our state," he says in one about how his parents taught him "[The
Golden Rule](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eeuHQ-A1B34)."

In the [second](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x7GCc3tgNoU), Pearson says,
"career politicians and the billionaires who control them want to convince us
that the problem is each other: white folk or Black folk, city folk or country
folk. Because as long as we're questioning our neighbors, we're not asking the
questions that matter."

"Why can't working families afford healthcare or groceries?" he asks. "And why
… are data centers being built in our backyards?"

Taylor's first [campaign
advertisement](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=4108748886082960) focuses on
how he's "tired of violent criminals running around Tennessee like squirrels
in a bait shop."

Back in Lawrence County, Marceaux worries about a [data
center](https://www.tennessean.com/picture-
gallery/news/local/2026/07/23/lawrenceburg-data-center-approved-resident-
backlash/90923628007/) planned for a property near her home. She is concerned
about the creek that runs near the data center's planned location, the well
water everyone in the area drinks and the swimming hole her grandchildren use.
She also worries about the potential impact on the bald eagles and a protected
species of heron found in the county. Previously, industries stripped a nearby
property of pine trees, she says, leading to a loss of woodpeckers.

"My hope [is] that [Pearson] can get up there and, on a higher level, he can
get us some protection, since our local governments don't want to protect us,"
she said.

## Gun Control, Affordability Cut Across Partisan Divisions

On a sunny Saturday in the town of Savannah, a group of six gathered
underneath the town gazebo before heading out to knock on doors across Hardin
County.

Kristina Richardson, volunteer lead for the county, said she first became
aware of Pearson when he was [temporarily
expelled](https://mlk50.com/2023/04/07/democracy-lost-but-justin-pearson-and-
justin-jones-will-be-back/) from the state legislature during the Covenant
School protest. A disabled veteran, she said she and her husband "are very
pro-Second Amendment," but want "commonsense gun laws." Pearson's protest
impressed her, she said.

Most Tennesseans--including Democrats, Republicans and a majority of self-
described "MAGA Republicans"--support tougher background checks for firearm
owners, according to a [2023 Vanderbilt University
poll](https://wpln.org/post/latest-vanderbilt-poll-finds-jump-in-support-
across-tennessee-for-more-gun-regulations/). Pearson supporters across
District 9 say his focus on gun control and affordability has helped him
broaden his appeal to more conservative voters.

Jenna Gammill, who grew up in Savannah and now lives in the adjacent Wayne
County, said the area is "bleeding red."

"Slowly but surely, there's people getting fed up, but they don't want to
crush their own ego and admit that they messed up," she said. "I'm hoping that
they'll maybe start to vote for things that will help them and not harm them."

Major issues include the lack of access to healthcare and the high cost of
diesel fuel for farmers, she said. She thinks more people will vote Democrat
in this election--even if they won't say so publicly.

Allie Stokes, who joined Richardson and Gammill to canvas, said when Pearson
visited Savannah in June, she heard him answer questions about environmental
concerns related to the Tennessee River, which flows through the town of
[fewer than 8,000
people](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/savannahcitytennessee/BZA110223).

"We can't even eat the fish out of the river here safely anymore on a regular
basis, because there are signs at the river that say it gives you cancer,"
Stokes said.

When someone brought that concern up to Pearson, he promised to look into it,
she said. He also seemed in touch with people struggling with the cost of
living, she said.

"I feel like he's going to be a representative that doesn't forget the people
that put him there when he gets in office," she said.

As the group knocked on doors around Hardin County, Stokes voiced surprise at
how many Democrat-voting households she saw.

"I'm really passionate about Justin's campaign," Stokes said. "I've seen him
speak, and it really seems like he cares about each part of the district that
he wants to represent, not just one demographic or one side of it."

## Pearson Supporters Say Coalition-Building Will Outlast Election

Now, Richardson is not only volunteering for Pearson's campaign, but also
joining a coalition of people from across the new District 9 who plan to
support their neighbors in times of need and advocate for progressive causes
even after the election.

Richardson sees some irony in it: Republicans meant to divide up Democrats in
creating the new District 9, but instead people are organizing across the 15
counties. "And we're willing to drive," she said.

Regardless of the outcome of this election, "I think [Pearson has] shown us
that we do have the power, even though they tried to take it by gerrymandering
the district," she said. "It's backfired on them, and it's brought us closer
together. It's got me talking to people two, three hours away from me and
working with them on this campaign, for instance, but also on other things
like the data center in Lawrenceburg."

Pearson said in an interview that as he's traveled the district, he's found
more commonality than differences, including among people who vote Independent
or Republican.

"It was a concern of mine that folks may not be as receptive to us: that the
racism that the state house was banking on, quite frankly, by rigging the
district this way would disadvantage us to the point where it'd be impossible.
But that's not what we're seeing," Pearson said. "I think our message is
reaching Republicans and conservative people because it is people-first
policies, and for anybody with a good conscience or goodwill, I think that
resonates."
